1: \section{What confidence transport did in the nonlinear study}
2: \label{sec:transport-followup}
3: 
4: Does a valid way to transport confidence also give useful decisions and
5: informative regret bounds?  We study this question in a controlled nonlinear
6: model.  Cumulative pseudo-regret measures the expected reward lost, over all
7: rounds, by choosing the learner's action instead of the best action for each
8: context.  Lower values are better.  In this study, the Hessian policy
9: has higher mean pseudo-regret than every comparator in every condition.
10: Its regret bounds, and those of the frozen reference policy, are larger than
11: a simple deterministic cap.  The recorded confidence and optimism checks
12: nevertheless pass.  The findings separate those numerical checks from the
13: practical usefulness of the resulting scores and bounds.
14: 
15: The prespecified follow-up evaluates 600 policy trajectories; a separate 294
16: development and tuning trajectories precede evaluation.  We fix
17: $T=1000$ and $W\in\{16,1,0.25\}$, with 50 common evaluation seeds per condition
18: and four policies.  The model parameter $W$ changes both the reward function
19: and its curvature, so comparisons across conditions do not isolate an effect
20: of metric drift.  The original near-linear study appears separately in
21: \Cref{sec:transport-instantiation}; its evidence is not pooled with this study.
22: 
23: The near-linear guarantee in \Cref{cor:global-near-linear-new} concerns a
24: family in which $W$ grows at least linearly with the horizon, with a
25: sufficiently large problem-dependent constant and the corollary's other
26: assumptions.  This study evaluates the stated fixed values of $W$ at a single
27: horizon.  It does not test that asymptotic scaling, and the numerical values
28: alone do not establish a violation of a theorem assumption.
29: 
30: \paragraph{What differs between the policies?}
31: All policies use the corrected center and confidence radius from
32: \Cref{cor:corrected-center-new}.  They differ in how they turn a width into an
33: exploration bonus.  \emph{Hessian} inflates the current width using the analytic
34: path certificate $\bar D_t^Q$.  It uses a bound on how prediction gradients
35: vary to control an auxiliary path joining the reference and current matrices.
36: This comparison path is not the optimizer's training path.  \emph{Endpoint}
37: replaces that path certificate with the dense endpoint Thompson distance:
38: it compares the reference and current matrices directly, without accumulating
39: changes along the auxiliary path.  \emph{Frozen reference} uses the
40: reference width directly.  \emph{Naive current} uses the current width without
41: transport and serves as an uncertified control.  All four policies update
42: their representations: ``frozen'' describes the metric's collection-time
43: gradients, not a fixed representation.  The policies receive matched contexts
44: and potential-noise streams, but their actions and subsequent learning
45: histories can differ.
46: 
47: \paragraph{Which policies incur less regret?}
48: \Cref{fig:transport-followup-outcomes} shows the higher mean regret of Hessian
49: transport in each condition; \Cref{tab:transport-followup-outcomes} gives the
50: numerical values.  The paired comparisons ask how much a comparator's regret
51: differs from Hessian's on the same evaluation seed.  All nine paired 95\%
52: intervals for this difference exclude zero in the comparator's favor.
53: These are pointwise intervals from 10,000 paired seed-bootstrap resamples per
54: comparison, without multiplicity adjustment.  They describe evaluation-seed
55: variation for the fixed teacher, design, and selected optimizer; they do not
56: include uncertainty from choosing the environment or tuning the optimizer.
57: Because policies follow their own adaptive histories, this comparison
58: measures the outcome of each complete policy.  It does not isolate the
59: effect of changing only a certificate at a fixed state or establish a
60: universal policy ordering.
61: 
62: For descriptive context, the online context-free mean-only benchmark has mean
63: regrets 185.26, 183.06, and 176.67 at $W=16,1,0.25$, respectively; the best fixed
64: action in hindsight has mean regrets 180.01, 177.97, and 171.84.  These means
65: use the same evaluation streams.  Hessian's sample means are close to the
66: context-free benchmark's, but no equivalence test was performed.  Similar
67: regret does not imply matching actions or identical use of context, and these
68: benchmarks do not bound the benefit available to another context-dependent
69: policy.  \Cref{app:transport-followup} defines both benchmarks.
70:

86: \paragraph{Do the regret bounds give useful information?}
87: We judge these regret bounds by whether they improve on what the reward
88: range already guarantees.  That range gives the deterministic regret cap
89: $2T\min(1,\sqrt W)$, which is 2000, 2000, and 1000 for the three conditions.
90: We call a larger bound \emph{vacuous}: it adds no information beyond the cap.
91: Every Hessian-policy bound is vacuous.  The frozen policy's own
92: reference-geometry bounds also exceed the caps in all 150 of its trajectories.
93: \Cref{fig:transport-followup-bound-scale} shows the size of their mean
94: right-hand sides relative to the cap.  The frozen policy's mean bounds are
95: much smaller than Hessian's, but neither provides a useful regret upper bound
96: in this study.
97: 
98: At $W=16,1,0.25$, the base-ten logarithms of
99: Hessian's mean terminal RHS divided by the cap are approximately 9.51, 37.19,
100: and 80.91.  The frozen policy's corresponding mean ratios, without taking
101: logarithms, are approximately 19, 60, and 231.  Each mean uses the named
102: policy's own 50 histories.  These summarize mean bound magnitudes; the
103: statement that every individual bound exceeds its cap is a separate check.
104: 
105: The largest contribution to the Hessian bounds is path inflation, the extra
106: charge introduced by the path certificate, in all three conditions.  This
107: explains their scale within the bound calculation, but
108: removing that term from Hessian's histories would not give the bound or
109: outcome of the frozen policy: the latter follows different histories.
110: The original near-linear study instead reported base-term dominance; that
111: description does not apply to this follow-up.

138: \paragraph{What did the confidence and drift checks show?}
139: The unfavorable policy outcomes did not coincide with a recorded failure of
140: the confidence or optimism checks.  The former check whether the reference
141: bands contain the true mean rewards; the latter check whether the action
142: scores upper-bound those means.  All 600 evaluation trajectories,
143: including naive current, pass the simultaneous reference-confidence,
144: method-optimism, and deterministic diagnostics.  Each policy--condition cell
145: has 50 successes out of 50, with an exact 95\% Clopper--Pearson interval of
146: approximately $[92.9\%,100\%]$.  These are observed checks, not proof of
147: population coverage or of the need for transport.  Float64 checks and
148: converged quadrature are numerical diagnostics; they do not verify the
149: theorem's assumptions through rigorous numerical enclosures.
150: 
151: There is measurable movement between the reference and current matrices.
152: The Hessian policy reaches endpoint distances above one in 16 of 50 seeds at
153: $W=0.25$, including 286 of 50,000 seed--round observations
154: (\Cref{tab:transport-followup-drift-bounds}).  These round counts describe
155: dependent observations, not additional independent replications.  The target
156: labels used to encode $W$ are not measured endpoint distances.
157: 
158: \paragraph{Model and implementation details.}
159: The observations are Gaussian with mean
160: $\mu_{\btheta}(z)=\sqrt W\tanh(\phi(z)^\top\btheta/\sqrt W)$,
161: with $\|\phi(z)\|_2\le1$ and projected parameters $\|\btheta\|_2\le1$.
162: Contexts have dimension four, there are five actions, and the context--action
163: feature map has dimension 29.  Noise has standard deviation $0.25$, the metric
164: ridge is one, and the confidence parameter is $\delta=0.05$.
165: A fixed teacher generates the rewards.  The conditions were specified before
166: their evaluation outcomes were observed.  Development, tuning, and evaluation
167: use disjoint seed sets.
168: 
169: The shared optimizer uses learning rate $3\times10^{-4}$ with 20 full-batch
170: steps followed by projection each round.  It was selected from nine
171: candidates by prediction MSE on uniform-random tuning histories.  This fixes
172: one implementation choice across policies; it does not establish
173: policy-specific regret-optimal tuning.  Dense float64 matrices and Cholesky
174: solves implement the exact-operator abstraction.  Actions are enumerated,
175: with ties resolved by the smallest action index.  This 29-parameter study
176: therefore examines dense numerical implementations.  It does not test
177: approximate solvers, large-model scalability, or real-data performance.
178: \Cref{app:transport-followup} records the protocol and provenance.
179: 
180: \paragraph{What do the recorded decisions reveal?}
181: After observing the policy outcomes, we examined how the Hessian score's
182: width bonus related to its recommendations.  We independently recomputed score
183: diagnostics from all 600 preserved trajectories.  On Hessian's own histories,
184: its selected action equals the current-width argmax on 99.382\%, 99.962\%, and 99.982\% of
185: rounds for $W=16,1,0.25$.  A stronger sufficient condition---the bonus gap
186: between the two largest widths exceeding the entire range of prediction
187: centers---holds on 97.104\%, 99.372\%, and 99.508\% of rounds.
188: Under this condition, differences in predicted reward cannot overturn the
189: largest-width action's bonus advantage.  Argmax agreement means that the
190: policy chooses the action ranked first by current width under the same tie
191: rule.  The stronger condition identifies states where the bonus gap alone
192: forces that choice.  The rounds are dependent, and this retrospective
193: calculation does not identify an adaptive causal mechanism.
194: 
195: The per-seed table in \Cref{app:transport-followup} evaluates this same Hessian
196: score on histories generated by all four policies.  Its non-Hessian rows
197: describe what Hessian would recommend on those states, not how the other
198: policies' own scores choose actions.  The appendix also compares alternative
